title: Judged on love
hookLine: John's saying: in the evening of life, we will be examined on love
tomorrow: how many ways can one poem say what prayer is?

lines: THEY DIDN'T KNOW IT WAS A TEST.
cards: Study guide, practice test, the night-before cram. Most exams at least tell you the subject. John of the Cross wrote one short line about the last exam of all, and he gave the subject away.
In his Spanish: "A la tarde te examinarán en el amor." In the evening, you will be examined on love. One subject.
And here's the odd part. In the Gospel scene behind that line, the people who pass have no idea they were ever taking the test.

teach.b: A king separates people, the way a shepherd separates sheep from goats, and tells one group why they're welcome: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in."
Sick, and you visited. In prison, and you came. And they're baffled.

"Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee?" They don't remember doing any of it for him. Then the answer: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."
Now the strange detail gets stranger.
The other group asks the very same question: when? Nobody on either side knew. So the puzzle solves itself.

The exam isn't on what you can recite under pressure. It's on what you did for whoever was in front of you, mostly without noticing. John's saying goes on, in a paraphrase: learn to love the way God wants to be loved.

teach.h: A VERDICT BECOMES A STUDY PLAN.
teach.b: That turns the verdict into a study plan.
Christians read Matthew 25 as a picture of the last judgment, and also as a map for this afternoon.

how: Many Christians end the day with an examination of conscience, looking back over the hours; Matthew 25's list of feeding, welcoming and visiting is also the root of what Catholics call the corporal works of mercy.

o: John's saying: life's last exam has one subject, love
a rule that confession must list sins against love first
a church court where monks were tried on their charity

games.q: the evening exam — tap the pairs.
p: ye have done it unto me
the hungry, the stranger, the sick

s: 'in the evening we will be examined on love' is a Bible verse
it's one of John of the Cross's short sayings. the Gospel scene behind it is Matthew 25.
in Matthew 25, the people welcomed by the king don't remember serving him
they ask, baffled: Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee?
only the people sent away ask 'when?'
both groups ask the same question. nobody on either side knew.

games.q: your cousin says, 'judgment day is basically a pop quiz on Bible facts.' you open Matthew 25. what does the king actually ask about?
o: the hungry fed, the stranger taken in, the sick visited.
which verses each person could recite from memory.
how often each person went to church services.
games.why: the king names meat, drink, a stranger taken in, the sick and the prisoner visited, and the people who did it didn't know it counted.

practice: Run back through today from the moment you woke. On your fingers, count the small moments someone needed something: a reply, a ride, a little patience. Don't grade them; just notice which ones you met and which slipped past.
If you pray, you can hand the whole day over, the slipped ones too.

wordCard.voice: Judged on love. John's evening exam: one subject, and the ones who pass never knew they were sitting it.

orig.note: Greek: the least. the king's word in Matthew 25:40 for the ones he calls his brethren.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: examined on love, a test you don't cram for because you're already sitting it. That's today.
